al-Ṭūsī says of the Sufis in al-Lumaʿ, p. 42: “They were named after the outward appearance of their clothing, not after any branch of knowledge or spiritual state by which they were known, because wearing wool was the practice of the prophets, peace be upon them, of the truthful, and the mark of poor worshippers.” In al-Kalābādhī’s al-Taʿarruf li-Madhhab al-Taṣawwuf (d. 380 AH/990 CE), Cairo ed., 1923, ch. 1, he says of the Sufis: “They were called Sufis because of their clothing and appearance. They did not wear, for the pleasure of the self, clothes that were soft to the touch or beautiful to look at. They dressed only to cover themselves, and so deliberately chose rough haircloth and coarse wool.” al-Kalābādhī also reports al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī as saying: “I met seventy men who had fought at Badr, and they wore nothing but wool.”↩︎

These ascetics could become so isolated from society that one of them would never leave his house, or would dig out a cellar where he secluded himself even from his own family. al-Iṣfahānī reports this in Ḥilyat al-Awliyāʾ (6/345) about ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-Rāsī, one of the ascetics of Basra.↩︎

The picture al-Masʿūdī gives us of social conditions at the end of the Umayyad period may help show what we mean by the development of social and political conflict. He reports that after the fall of the Umayyad state, one of its elders was asked why it had collapsed. He answered: “We became so occupied with our pleasures that we neglected what we were obliged to watch over. We wronged our subjects, so they lost hope of justice from us. Our officials mistreated them, so they longed to be rid of us. We burdened the taxpayers, so they abandoned us. Our estates were ruined, and with them our treasuries. We trusted our ministers, and they put their own interests before ours. They carried out affairs without us and hid knowledge of them from us. The pay of our soldiers was delayed, so they stopped obeying us. Our enemy called them over, and they joined him in fighting us. Our enemies came after us, and we were unable to resist because we had so few supporters...” The words may not really have been spoken by an Umayyad, but the picture they paint accurately reflects the historical reality of the final days of the Umayyad state. See al-Masʿūdī, Murūj al-Dhahab, vol. 2, p. 194.↩︎

The ideological side of this practice lies in its preparing the way for what the Sufis later called walāya, or sainthood. The Sufis created this rank for those among them who reached the highest spiritual stations, and attributed to their “saints” divine wonders similar to the miracles of prophets. The real basis of this Sufi idea of sainthood was an attempt to take absolute religious authority away from the caliphs, whose monopoly on the title “God’s caliph and His shadow on earth” formed part of the official religious ideology of the caliphate. The creation of Sufi sainthood was therefore one of many different ways in which the ideology of the state was challenged.↩︎

The Arabs conquered Khurasan by treaty in 30 AH/650 CE, during the caliphate of ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān. But revolts and other forms of resistance to Arab rule continued through almost the entire Umayyad period, and then returned under the Abbasids in many new forms, including intellectual and ideological ones. Under al-Manṣūr, the people of Khurasan revolted against him in 136 AH/753 CE. See Murūj al-Dhahab, vol. 2, p. 237.↩︎
Khurasan was one of the main centers of the Alids and later of Abbasid propaganda against the Umayyads. It remained an important center of Shiʿism throughout Islamic history.↩︎

During the caliphate of the Umayyad Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik (105–125 AH/723–742 CE), for example, the people of Khurasan took an active part in the revolt of Zayd ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib in 121 AH/738 CE. See Ibn al-Ṭiqṭaqā, al-Fakhrī fī al-Ādāb al-Sulṭāniyya, p. 113. Historians have usually explained revolts like this purely in sectarian terms—as expressions of Shiʿism—while neglecting their social motives. Yet for many participants, the main motives were less sectarian than they were forms of resistance to social or political domination. This applies very clearly to the people of Khurasan at the time.↩︎

Sufi sources tell us that Ibrāhīm ibn Adham lived in Basra, Alexandria, and Mecca and later in Syria. See Ṭabaqāt al-Ṣūfiyya, p. 30. They say that al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ went to Kufa and lived there; see Jāmī, Nafaḥāt al-Uns, p. 38. He died in 187 AH/803 CE; see Ibn al-Jawzī, Ṣifat al-Ṣafwa, vol. 2, p. 134. Ibn al-Mubārak left Khurasan for Kufa; see ibid., vol. 4, p. 109. The sources disagree over the journeys, beliefs, and fate of Shaqīq al-Balkhī. The author of al-Kawākib al-Durriyya (vol. 1, p. 121) says that he once set out accompanied by 300 poor worshippers and ascetics, and that he met the Abbasid caliph al-Maʾmūn and admonished him. Nafaḥāt al-Uns (p. 15) presents him as Sunni, while Rawḍāt al-Jannāt (p. 328) presents him as a Jaʿfari and says that he was martyred in Transoxiana on a charge of rafḍ, or Shiʿism. Nafaḥāt al-Uns (p. 50) says that he was martyred in the province of Khuttal, and so on.↩︎

By the “social dimension” of Khurasani asceticism at the time, we mean that in its real historical basis it grew mainly out of resistance to official Arab institutions. That resistance mixed “national” feeling with reactions against social and political oppression.↩︎

The term commonly used by the early Sufis was maḥabba, “love.” In Sufi teaching and practice, love was counted among the “states.” They defined a “state” as “something that descends into the heart, or with which the heart becomes adorned through the purity of remembrance.” See al-Sarrāj al-Ṭūsī, al-Lumaʿ, p. 66.↩︎
See al-Shaybī, al-Ṣila bayna al-Taṣawwuf wa-l-Tashayyuʿ, pp. 298–299.↩︎

If we set aside the miraculous elements, we can draw the following picture from what ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Badawī cites from Farīd al-Dīn ʿAṭṭār’s Persian Tadhkirat al-Awliyāʾ—Nicholson ed., Leiden and London, 1905 and 1907, vol. 1, pp. 59–61—and from the Arabic sources: Ibn Khallikān, Wafayāt al-Aʿyān, vol. 1, p. 256, Cairo, 1858; Ibn Taghrībirdī, al-Nujūm al-Zāhira, vol. 1, p. 33, Cairo, 1929; al-Jāḥiẓ, al-Bayān wa-l-Tabyīn, vol. 3, p. 85, Cairo, 1332 AH; and al-Jāḥiẓ, al-Ḥayawān, vol. 1, p. 78, Cairo, 1907. Rābiʿa al-ʿAdawiyya was born into a very poor family in Basra and was connected to Banū ʿAdwa through clientage rather than descent. When she was still young, her father died and a famine struck Basra. She and her three sisters became separated and wandered without direction. A cruel man captured her and sold her for six dirhams to a man who worked her very hard. One day, as she was walking, she noticed a man looking at her with bad intentions and ran away. On the road she threw herself onto the ground and prayed to God. She then heard a voice say: “Do not grieve. On the Day of Judgment, those closest to God in heaven will look toward you and envy what you will become.” After hearing this, she returned to her “master’s” house, began fasting, continued serving him, and spent the whole night in prayer. See Badawī, Shahīdat al-ʿIshq al-Ilāhī, Cairo, 1962, 2nd ed., pp. 8, 12. Even this summary still contains a legendary element at the end of the story.↩︎

By these elements we mean sayings attributed to Rābiʿa that are also attributed to other people. For example, she is reported to have said: “I did not worship Him [God] out of fear of His fire, or out of desire for His paradise, for then I would be like a bad hired worker. I worshipped Him out of love for Him and longing for Him.” See al-Manāwī, al-Kawākib al-Durriyya, vol. 1, p. 109. The same idea, and sometimes the same wording, is often attributed to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, and also to his grandson ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn; see ibid. Rābiʿa is also said to have remarked: “How many desires have lost their pleasure while leaving their burden behind with me.” Ibid. Almost the same words are also attributed to the Kufan ascetic ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtba al-Hudhalī, who died around 110 AH/728 CE; see Ibn al-Jawzī, Ṣifat al-Ṣafwa, vol. 3, p. 56.
